articles.title: Rinoceronte ameaçado é flagrado atacando carro com turista | G1
articles.standfirst: Motorista realizava passeio por conta própria, sem motorista ou monitores especializados, na Namíbia.
articles.summary: Motorista realizava passeio por conta própria, sem motorista ou monitores especializados, na Namíbia.
articles.body:
Um rinoceronte-negro, espécie criticamente ameaçada de extinção, investiu contra o carro de um turista e o danificou com seu chifre durante um safári autoguiado na Namíbia .

Funcionários da empresa de turismo Etosha Salt Pan Adventure assistiram, chocados, ao desenrolar do incidente aterrorizante no Parque Nacional de Etosha, em 19 de setembro.

O rinoceronte investe repetidamente contra o veículo, cravando o chifre na lataria e danificando o carro; ao fundo, ouve-se um funcionário — que filmava a cena de outro veículo — instando o motorista, em francês, a fugir e criticando sua permanência no local.

Rinoceronte ameaçado de extinção ataca veículo durante safári — Foto: Reprodução/Reuters

No vídeo, ouve-se o motorista que está ao lado do cinegrafista dizer: "Ele [o motorista do veículo atacado] não está entendendo agora. Ele vê um animal desorientado assim, uma vez na vida, e fica paralisado. Ele está bem aqui. Aí está."

"Ele já deveria ter ido embora. É só exibição."

A gravação foi feita por um cliente da empresa de safári, que alertou outros visitantes sobre os perigos associados aos rinocerontes-negros.

O gerente declarou: "Este é um lembrete contundente de que um safári autoguiado não é uma visita a um zoológico."

"O vídeo registra o momento em que um rinoceronte-negro atacou um turista que dirigia seu próprio carro dentro do parque . Animais selvagens podem parecer calmos em um instante e tornar-se extremamente perigosos no momento seguinte."

A empresa informou que o rinoceronte havia dado sinais de alerta antes do ataque, mas os ocupantes do carro não os perceberam.

Eles acrescentaram: "Rinocerontes frequentemente dão sinais de alerta, especialmente os rinocerontes-negros, mas é importante não considerar esses sinais como uma garantia de segurança. Um rinoceronte-negro pode reagir muito rapidamente, principalmente se for surpreendido ou se sentir ameaçado ."

A empresa recomendou aos visitantes que contratem guias locais experientes e sigam as normas do parque.

O rinoceronte-negro ( Diceros bicornis ) está classificado como "criticamente ameaçado" na Lista Vermelha da IUCN, e a Namíbia abriga uma das maiores populações remanescentes da espécie.

articles.title: São José dos Campos terá IPTU 100% digital a partir de 2027 | G1
articles.standfirst: Mudança permitirá acesso aos carnês pelo site da Prefeitura ou por e-mail e deve reduzir o uso de papel e os custos de impressão e envio.
articles.summary: Mudança permitirá acesso aos carnês pelo site da Prefeitura ou por e-mail e deve reduzir o uso de papel e os custos de impressão e envio.
articles.body:
A partir de 2027, os contribuintes de São José dos Campos terão uma nova forma de acessar o carnê do IPTU. A Prefeitura oficializou o programa IPTU Digital, que estabelece a emissão 100% digital dos carnês, da taxa de coleta de lixo e da contribuição de iluminação pública e segurança.

Com a mudança, o contribuinte poderá emitir o carnê diretamente pelo site da Prefeitura, tanto para pagamento à vista quanto parcelado. Também será possível solicitar o recebimento por e-mail, mediante cadastro antecipado, ou realizar a emissão presencialmente em um dos protocolos regionais.

A iniciativa foi oficializada pelo Decreto Municipal 20.344/2026, publicado no Diário do Município em agosto. A medida consolida um processo de digitalização que começou em 2021, quando a Prefeitura passou a oferecer a opção de recebimento do carnê por e-mail. Desde então, as alternativas digitais foram ampliadas.

Além de facilitar o acesso aos documentos e ao pagamento dos tributos, o IPTU Digital contribui para a redução do uso de papel e dos custos relacionados à impressão e ao envio dos carnês pelos Correios.

Até este ano, a Prefeitura realizou a impressão de 234 mil carnês, encaminhados aos contribuintes pelos Correios. Outros 34.705 carnês foram enviados por e-mail a pessoas que já haviam solicitado essa opção. Com a digitalização integral, o município passa a adotar um modelo mais prático, econômico e sustentável para a emissão dos documentos.

A mudança reforça a ampliação dos serviços digitais oferecidos pela Prefeitura de São José dos Campos, permitindo que o contribuinte tenha acesso ao carnê de forma rápida e diretamente pelos canais oficiais do município.

articles.title: Mãe que atribui morte do filho a bets comemora proibição no Brasil | G1
articles.standfirst: Vânia de Souza Borges, de Uberlândia, se reuniu com Lula e pediu que governo ‘cortasse o mal pela raiz’. Rafael Borges Amaral morreu em 2024, aos 26 anos; mãe atribui morte à dependência em apostas.
articles.summary: Após perder o filho para o vício em apostas online, Vânia Borges celebra a proibição de bets no Brasil e pede punição rigorosa para o setor em novo projeto.
articles.body:
Por quase dois anos, Vânia de Souza Borges transformou o luto pela morte do filho em uma campanha contra as apostas on-line . Nesta sexta-feira (25), ao saber que o governo federal anunciou medidas para proibir as bets e os jogos virtuais on-line no Brasil, a professora de Uberlândia , no Triângulo Mineiro, diz ter sentido alívio, mas não considera a luta encerrada. Ela atribui a morte do filho às bets.

A medida veio poucos dias depois dela se sentar frente a frente com o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), em Brasília . No encontro, no domingo (13), Vânia levou a história do filho, Rafael Borges Amaral, morto em 2024 aos 26 anos, e fez um pedido direto: que o governo não se limitasse a regulamentar o setor.

“Estou aliviada, mas sei que é apenas o começo da luta”, afirmou Vânia ao g1.

Na ocasião, a professora junto com mais sete pessoas que se declaram dependentes de apostas, foram compartilhar com o presidente da República a realidade de quem é impactado pelos danos causados por esse tipo de vício.

“Falei que a solução é cortar o mal pela raiz, é acabar com as bets. Falei que regulamentar não basta, teria que acabar definitivamente”, contou à época.

Agora, diante do anúncio do governo, ela diz enxergar um primeiro resultado concreto de uma mobilização que começou depois da morte de Rafael.

“Ao longo dessa trajetória eu mudei muito, a Vânia de antes que muitas vezes não foi ouvida, comemora em saber que finalmente algo começa a ser feito. Sinto que o Lula entendeu quando eu disse que é preciso cortar o mal pela raiz”, afirmou.

O governo anunciou nesta sexta um pacote que determina a interrupção das apostas on-line no país. Segundo o governo, os apostadores poderão retirar voluntariamente os valores disponíveis nas plataformas até as 23h59 de 5 de outubro. A partir de 6 de outubro, os sites e aplicativos deverão sair do ar.

Até 23:59 de 5 de outubro: Apostadores vão ter que retirar saldos das plataformas

A partir do dia 6 de outubro: Os sites e aplicativos saem do ar

Entre os dias 7 e 8 de outubro: Informação dos saldos por CPF

Entre os dias 9 a 14 de outubro: Devolução integral dos saldos

A partir do dia 14 de outubro: Em caso de impedimento, a Caixa Econômica Federal intermediará a devolução aos apostadores

O Executivo também prepara um projeto de lei para criar crimes relacionados à exploração e operação das chamadas bets, além de punições para atividades como publicidade, recrutamento de apostadores e determinadas formas de intermediação financeira. A proposta ainda precisa ser analisada pelo Congresso. Saiba mais abaixo.

Para Vânia, a mudança anunciada ultrapassa a história da própria família.

“Essa não é uma conquista apenas para mim, mas de todas as mães que passam ou passaram pelo que passei”, disse.

Ela afirma que ainda pretende entender os detalhes das medidas anunciadas pelo governo antes de definir os próximos passos da mobilização.

“Agora quero entender melhor como tudo vai funcionar”, afirmou.

Rafael Borges Amaral morreu em 23 de março de 2024, em Uberlândia. O boletim de ocorrência registrou a morte como suicídio. Vânia sustenta que a dependência em apostas on-line teve papel determinante no desfecho.

Segundo a mãe, as apostas passaram a ocupar uma parte cada vez maior da rotina do filho, afetando o trabalho, a renda e as relações pessoais. Pouco antes de morrer, ele teria enviado um áudio a um amigo dizendo que não conseguia mais controlar as apostas e as perdas financeiras.

Vânia também afirma ter encontrado uma transferência de R$ 30 feita por Rafael, na madrugada do dia da morte, para uma conta vinculada à empresa responsável pelo chamado 'Jogo do Tigrinho'.

Depois da morte, ela procurou o Ministério Público e a Polícia Civil para pedir investigação. Em maio de 2025, segundo a família, o Ministério Público de Minas Gerais determinou o arquivamento da investigação.

A professora, porém, continuou reunindo documentos, áudios e e-mails do filho e cobrando medidas contra as plataformas e os influenciadores que promovem apostas. Uma carta escrita por ela chegou a ser anexada aos documentos da CPI das Bets no Senado.

Após acessar o celular e a caixa de e-mails de Rafael, Vânia encontrou dezenas de mensagens promocionais de plataformas de apostas — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Atualmente, as apostas de quota fixa são reguladas pela Secretaria de Prêmios e Apostas do Ministério da Fazenda; desde janeiro de 2025, somente empresas autorizadas pelo governo podem operar nacionalmente.

A nova ofensiva, segundo o governo, faz parte de um pacote voltado ao combate ao endividamento das famílias e inclui também medidas contra o mercado ilegal de apostas.

Para Vânia, porém, o anúncio desta sexta não encerra a história. É, como ela própria resumiu, o começo de uma nova etapa.

O g1 teve acesso à minuta do projeto que deve ser enviado ao Congresso pelo Executivo.

🚔De acordo com a minuta da proposta, explorar ou operar as chamadas 'apostas de quota fixa', por qualquer meio, passará a ser crime punido com reclusão de 4 a 6 anos, além de multa.

A punição será aplicada mesmo que o agente tenha autorização de uma autoridade estrangeira.

A proposta prevê estender as mesmas penas a quem oferece, recebe, registra, faz a intermediação, disponibiliza ou administra canais e estabelecimentos de apostas.

A punição, se o texto for aprovado pelo Congresso, será aumentada de um terço caso o objeto da aposta seja um evento virtual de jogo on-line, como os populares cassinos virtuais, caso do 'jogo do tigrinho'.

Além da exploração direta, o projeto que deve ser enviado ao Legislativo criminaliza atividades relacionadas às bets:

Divulgação e publicidade: fazer propaganda, publicidade ou marketing para incentivar apostas terá pena de reclusão de 2 a 4 anos, e multa. A mesma sanção será aplicada sobre quem recruta apostadores ou monetiza esse tipo de publicidade. O texto ressalta, contudo, que o formato não se aplicará a conteúdos de natureza jornalística, informativa, educativa, acadêmica, científica ou crítica.

Uso de dados pessoais: o fornecimento, comercialização ou segmentação de listas de dados pessoais com a finalidade de direcionar publicidade de apostas também será punido com reclusão de 2 a 4 anos, com agravantes caso os dados envolvam o histórico de perdas dos apostadores, transtornos de jogo diagnosticados ou informações de crianças e adolescentes.

Facilitação financeira e plataformas: instituições ou agentes que realizem transações, processamento ou armazenamento de pagamentos de apostas, sabendo de sua proveniência, bem como desenvolvedores e distribuidores de aplicativos e plataformas de apostas online, também poderão ser submetidos a penas de 2 a 4 anos de reclusão.

Rafael com a família — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

A deputada federal Dandara (PT-MG) protocolou uma representação no Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública para que a Secretaria Nacional do Consumidor (Senacon) e o Departamento de Proteção e Defesa do Consumidor apurem possíveis práticas de publicidade enganosa, estratégias digitais consideradas predatórias e falhas na proteção de usuários das plataformas de apostas.

Além da representação ao Ministério da Justiça, a deputada também apresentou dois projetos de lei relacionados ao mercado de apostas, apelidados de 'PLs Rafael'.

Um deles proíbe que influenciadores e afiliados sejam remunerados com base nas perdas financeiras dos apostadores atraídos por suas publicidades. Pela proposta, eles só poderão receber valores fixos por campanhas, sem vínculo com depósitos, apostas ou prejuízos dos usuários.

O segundo projeto obriga as plataformas de apostas a monitorar o comportamento dos usuários para identificar sinais de compulsão.

Caso sejam detectados indícios de dependência, as empresas deverão comunicar a Secretaria de Prêmios e Apostas, que poderá determinar o bloqueio temporário da conta por, no mínimo, 60 dias.

Durante esse período, o apostador não poderá receber publicidade ou bônus de incentivo e deverá ser orientado sobre canais de apoio psicológico.

Os dois projetos aguardam o início da tramitação na Câmara dos Deputados.

articles.body:
Santos terá interdições de ruas e avenidas por toda a cidade durante o próximo sábado (26). — Foto: Prefeitura de Santos

Santos , no litoral de São Paulo, terá interdições de ruas e avenidas em razão de cinco eventos programados para sábado (26), em diferentes pontos da cidade. Linhas municipais de transporte coletivo também seguirão por rotas alternativas.

articles.standfirst: Cidade criou 494 vagas com carteira assinada em julho e acumula 2.712 novos empregos formais nos primeiros sete meses de 2026.
articles.summary: Cidade criou 494 vagas com carteira assinada em julho e acumula 2.712 novos empregos formais nos primeiros sete meses de 2026.
articles.body:
São José dos Campos mantém um cenário positivo na geração de empregos e reforça sua força econômica. Em julho, a cidade registrou 494 novos postos de trabalho com carteira assinada , resultado da diferença entre contratações e desligamentos no período.

O desempenho mantém uma sequência de resultados positivos no mercado de trabalho. Julho foi o sétimo mês consecutivo em que São José registrou mais contratações do que demissões , consolidando uma trajetória de crescimento ao longo de 2026.

Com o resultado de julho, o município chegou a 2.712 novos empregos formais criados nos primeiros sete meses do ano . Nos últimos 12 meses, o saldo também permanece positivo, com 1.926 novas vagas. Ao todo, São José conta atualmente com 214.042 trabalhadores com carteira assinada .

O setor de serviços foi o principal destaque de julho, responsável pela criação de 355 vagas. A indústria também apresentou desempenho positivo, com 138 novos postos, seguida pela construção civil, com 95, e pelo setor agropecuário, com cinco.

Os números refletem a diversidade da economia joseense e a capacidade do município de gerar oportunidades em diferentes segmentos. O resultado também reforça a importância de um ambiente favorável à atividade econômica, à inovação e ao desenvolvimento de empresas.

A sequência de resultados positivos mostra que São José dos Campos segue mantendo seu mercado de trabalho aquecido. Com mais de 2,7 mil novos empregos formais gerados somente em 2026 , a cidade demonstra capacidade de criar oportunidades e sustentar uma trajetória de desenvolvimento econômico.

articles.standfirst: Evento acontece no sábado (26), em Porto Feliz (SP), e marca o lançamento do Boa Vista Estates, empreendimento que integra o Complexo Boa Vista, considerado refúgio de famosos e bilionários no interior de São Paulo
articles.summary: Shania Twain se apresenta no lançamento do Boa Vista Estates, em Porto Feliz, marcando seu retorno ao país após oito anos em um evento restrito para convidados.
articles.body:
Shania Twain encantou e faz história na Arena da Festa do Peão de Barretos em sua última passagem pelo Brasil — Foto: Érico Andrade/G1

A cantora canadense Shania Twain retorna ao Brasil, após oito anos, para um show exclusivo para convidados em um empreendimento de alto luxo em Porto Feliz (SP), no sábado (26). O show marca a apresentação do Boa Vista Estates, empreendimento que integra o Complexo Boa Vista, considerado refúgio de famosos e bilionários no interior do estado.

A cantora esteve no Brasil há oito anos, quando se apresentou na Arena da Festa do Peão de Barretos (SP) . Na ocasião, ela fez o público cantar a plenos pulmões “Come on Over”, música que dá nome ao seu disco de maior sucesso e que a tornou conhecida em todo o mundo. O álbum deu a ela quatro prêmios Grammy e o topo das paradas musicais mais importantes do mundo.

Conforme a JHSF, dona do empreendimento que será lançado na ocasião do show, o Boa Vista Estates tem Valor Geral de Vendas (VGV) potencial estimado em cerca de R$ 3 bilhões e amplia a proposta do complexo, que completa 20 anos em 2027, ao reunir terrenos de grandes extensões, infraestrutura completa e uma ocupação cuidadosamente planejada para um número reduzido de famílias.

A área dedicada é de 7 milhões de metros quadrados no total, distribuídos entre ruas privadas, lagos, áreas de lazer e mata nativa. O local foi projetado para receber 250 famílias, priorizando máxima privacidade, conforto e integração com a paisagem campestre.

As estâncias, com áreas a partir de 20.000 m², e os lotes, a partir de 5.000 m², estão distribuídos ao longo de ruas privadas, com vistas para os lagos, jardins e paisagens da região, garantindo independência entre as áreas residenciais.

O local do show fica a uma hora da capital, próximo da Rodovia Castello Branco, e não será aberto ao público em geral.

articles.title: Renan Santos defende reforma da Previdência e concessões em MG | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato à Presidência da República pelo Missão esteve em Uberaba, no Triângulo Mineiro, na tarde desta sexta-feira (25). Ele também falou sobre o SUS e a educação superior.
articles.summary: Em visita a Uberaba, o candidato Renan Santos detalhou propostas para a reforma da Previdência, concessões de rodovias e mudanças no SUS e no ensino superior.
articles.body:
Candidato à Presidência da República Renan Santos visitou o Mercado Municipal de Uberaba. — Foto: TV Integração/Reprodução

O candidato à Presidência da República Renan Santos (Missão) afirmou que fará uma reforma da Previdência e adotará o modelo de concessões para rodovias brasileiras durante visita a Uberaba , no Triângulo Mineiro, na tarde desta sexta-feira (25).

"Vai ter que reformar. Eu já estou avisando para todo mundo que o candidato que falar que não vai reformar a Previdência estará mentindo e vai enganar você. Vão votar achando que vai fazer uma coisa e ele vai entregar outra. Precisamos começar a fazer uma reforma paramétrica nos servidores públicos, especialmente federais, militares e ligados ao judiciário", disse.

No Mercado Municipal, ele também afirmou que pretende ampliar as concessões de rodovias.

"É o melhor modelo que tem. Você tem que combinar investimento público com o investimento privado. Hoje, a maior parte do investimento em infraestrutura no Brasil pode ser privado. O modelo de concessões é funcional. Naturalmente, você tem que ter meios regulatórios claros para não ter malandragens".

Renan Santos defendeu a adoção de um prontuário eletrônico único no Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS), em que o paciente poderá acompanhar todo o tratamento. Ele também propôs acabar com a fila por ordem de chegada e dar prioridade aos casos mais graves.

"Vamos fazer um prontuário único eletrônico que o paciente vai poder acompanhar pela internet ou aplicativo toda a sua trajetória. Isso vai fazer com que a fila de exame seja racionalizada. Uma pessoa que tem uma doença mais grave vai passar na frente. Uma pessoa que tem uma doença incapacitante que não pode voltar a trabalhar também passará na frente".

O candidato também falou sobre mudanças no ensino superior. Segundo ele, é preciso acabar com a autonomia universitária.

"Hoje a gente não pode entregar para os diretores das universidades a capacidade de escolher quais cursos vão ter prioridade e o Brasil não participar dessas escolhas. Se o Brasil está pagando a conta, nós temos que escolher o que que vai ser ensinado", finalizou.

articles.title: 'The blockade is complete': Locals flee occupied south Ukraine as hunger deepens
articles.summary: One Ukrainian official told ABC News that Oleshky has become "hell on earth."
articles.body:
Editor's note: This story contains graphic descriptions of wartime injuries and fatalities.

The southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky -- under Russian occupation since 2022 -- has become "hell on earth," local officials and humanitarian workers told ABC News, as thousands of remaining residents face starvation and hundreds flee through a war zone littered with mines and bodies.

Oleshky is located close to the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, which since Ukraine's liberation of the city of Kherson in the fall of 2022 has formed the frontline between Ukrainian and Russian forces in the southern theater.

Recent weeks have seen voices from the city and its surrounding rural communities emerge anew as Ukrainian officials and humanitarian organizations seek to bring attention to the deteriorating situation on the Dnipro's left bank, in view of the Ukrainian forces holding their positions only a few miles away along the right bank.

Tetiana Hasanenko, a Ukrainian official serving from the western side of the Dnipro as the head of the Oleshky Military Administration, told ABC News that the area's prewar population of around 40,000 people has fallen to as low as 6,000, with only around 2,000 in Oleshky city.

Those who remain, she said, face rapidly deteriorating living conditions and a Russian occupation authority with little apparent interest in alleviating them. "We are not talking about them surviving the winter," Hasanenko said.

Messages sent by residents in Oleshky and shared with ABC News tell of careful rationing of remaining food supplies, a chronic shortage of medication and having to move from one abandoned house to the next to escape drone attacks and marauding Russian troops.

"The blockade is complete," said one message. "Endless drones, fires. Like a horror movie."

Kseniia Arkhipova, a volunteer based on the Ukrainian-controlled side of the river who says she helps coordinate those hoping to flee, told ABC News that a recent collapse of food supplies prompted a new wave of evacuees.

A letter-writing campaign in the spring created enough attention, Arkhipova said, to push occupation forces to demine some of the local roads and allow supplies to reach Oleshky, where residents had been surviving thanks in part to produce grown in their own gardens.

Prices for basic goods were sky-high, and few people even had money to buy things with, she said. But they survived the summer.

On Sept. 1, though, a food-supply convoy heading to the city was attacked. Russian officials blamed the Ukrainian armed forces for the attack, while Kyiv blamed Moscow's troops.

"They were blown up. And then they were shot," Arkhipova said of the incident. "Then the drones flew in and attacked so that the drivers remained alive, just hit the motors so that the oil leaked out. Drivers then walked back by foot for 100 kilometers."

After that, she said, more locals began to leave the only way they could -- on foot. "Because there is simply nothing to eat. While there was something to eat, people just stayed in their homes," Arkhipova said.

To escape, residents must first reach the village of Radensk, some 14 miles east of Oleshky deeper into Russian-held territory, Arkhipova said. Hasanenko described the route as the "road of death," citing the mines and drones that cover the entire area.

In Radensk, those fleeing may be able to get food and a night's accommodation. The roads in that area are still mined and dangerous, Arkhipova added, but those fleeing may be able to catch a lift in a local's car or tractor to get further into occupied Kherson and closer to the Black Sea coast, from where they may be able to arrange -- usually at high cost -- a circuitous route to Ukrainian-held territory, often through Belarus.

Some are even helped by Russian volunteers, Arkhipova said, who buy them train tickets and accompany them on their route.

It can cost as much as $500 per person to flee, the money going toward the costs of food, accommodation and payment for whatever driver is willing to take them, Arkhipova said, adding that she has so far helped 47 people out.

But those fleeing face myriad dangers from the very start of their journey -- mines, FPV drones and Russian checkpoints among them. Those walking the road to Radensk "follow each other step by step" to dodge mines, Arkhipova said.

Many have already lost their identity documents, whether in the flames of war or in the devastating flooding that swamped the Kherson region after Russian forces blew up the Kakhovka dam in June 2023. Officials in Moscow and occupied Ukraine denied Russia's responsibility for the incident, though many experts said Russian troops were most likely responsible.

Those stopped at Russian checkpoints face interrogation and possible detention. "They interrogated a girl for four hours," Arkhipova said of one evacuee. "She said, 'I don't have my passport, everything burned down. There was an attack on the house.' They said, 'No, you are a spy.'"

While fierce combat has been ongoing along the banks of the Dnipro for years, Arkhipova said there is little organization behind the Russian lines.

"There's no leadership there," she said. "There are only [Russian] soldiers who openly say they don't care, 'We came here to earn money.'"

Russian forces reach the area through village roads, ever wary of Ukrainian drones and artillery. They bring in ammunition and weapons, using them to attack the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson on the right bank of the river, according to Ukrainian military officials.

"They don't let people go on these village roads that are not mined," Arkhipova said, for fear of residents seeing "where the trenches are, where the ammunition, cannons, self-propelled artillery mounts and everything else are." Anyone suspected of being in contact with Ukrainian authorities or armed forces faces immediate execution, Ukrainian officials say.

When the Russians come to the occupied settlements, Arkhipova added, they steal food and evict people from their homes -- particularly homes that have electricity, solar panels or a generator. "They kick the old people out," she said.

"They live there, exist for a while. They move around the city by foot, and Ukrainian drones are chasing them," she added of the Russian troops. "Then their corpses are lying on the street. These corpses are eaten by dogs."

Even Oleshky's hospital, a last lifeline for those still living there, "is on its last breath," Arkhipova said. "If the hospital closes, the city will die. There is no fuel in the hospital. There is no medicine." Those still staffing the facility do what they can, she added, "but it only prolongs the agony" of those they treat.

Hasanenko painted an apocalyptic picture of what remains of the city. "People lie on the road, rot, unburied. More than 100 corpses lie in the basement of the hospital today -- a hospital that has had no electricity for four years. And imagine what kind of stench is there from the hospital, in the city and around."

All of occupied Kherson remains an active war zone. For the Ukrainian military, responsibility for the Oleshky area falls to the 30th Marine Corps.

Its spokesperson, Pavlo Drogal, told ABC News that the unit's drones carefully track developments on the left bank. "There is a huge deficit of drinking water, electricity, food products," he said. "We observe this picture every day ... The situation from the drone looks really depressing."

Ukrainian drone operators track Russian troops operating in the area, Drogal said, and see them looting homes, sheltering in civilian areas, wearing civilian clothes and masking military vehicles in civilian colors.

Drogal said Ukrainian units do not engage in remote mining of the logistical routes or any other areas on the occupied left bank. "The enemy conducts mining there," he said. "We do not attack our own people."

"Does the enemy provoke? Yes. Do they fire on humanitarian transports? Yes. Do they allow humanitarian transports with humanitarian aid to Oleshky? No, they do not allow. We observe this all," he said.

As for the danger of collateral damage, Drogal responded, "We make our strikes, knowing exactly why we make these strikes. We strike only at representatives of the Russian occupation troops."

This week, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha raised the situation in Oleshky at the United Nations General Assembly high-level week in New York. In a statement published on Monday, Sybiha warned of a "humanitarian catastrophe" and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as "the only obstacle."

"Russia is deliberately making life there impossible," Sybiha said in an address during the UNGA. "They are starving them to death."

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov this month acknowledged the "critical situation" in Oleshky but accused Ukrainian forces of blocking humanitarian supplies intended for its residents.

Hasanenko and other Ukrainian officials have been trying to rally attention and action for several months, she said. Oleksandr Tolokonnikov -- the deputy head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration -- told ABC News earlier this month that the city has become "hell on earth."

"People in Oleshky are dying almost every day for lack of food, medical care, heart attacks and Russian shelling," Tolokonnikov added, also accusing Russian forces of using locals as "target practice" for drones, as Moscow's forces have been documented doing on the Ukrainian-held Kherson.

Some 300 people are waiting to evacuate, Arkhipova said, with 47 having already left in September. Any effort to facilitate a relief of the city demands the demining of the roads, the pausing of all shelling between the combatants and a convoy of humanitarian buses to take hundreds of people at once, she added.

But Arkhipova said she has little hope of a breakthrough. "I don't care. They are all useless," she said of officials, high-level international bodies and NGOs agitating on Oleshky's behalf. During previous humanitarian visits, she recalled, "They only spend my time and reassure people. They don't do anything else."

Even in the case of relief, some Oleshky residents likely will not leave, Arkhipova said. "They are ready to live and die in their homes. That's what they tell me: 'I'm not going anywhere. This is my home. Why should I leave my home?'"

articles.title: Inquest date set for toddler found with dead father in Skegness
articles.summary: A four-week jury inquest into the death of Bronson Battersby is due to begin on 22 February 2027.
articles.body:
An inquest into the death of a toddler who was discovered with his dead father is set to start in February next year.

Two-year-old Bronson Battersby and his father, Kenneth Battersby, 60, were found at a property in Skegness on 9 January 2024.

A fifth pre-inquest review at the Myle Cross Centre in Lincoln heard a four-week jury inquest was scheduled to begin on 22 February 2027.

Jayne Wilkes, area coroner for Greater Lincolnshire, also requested that any outstanding evidence be submitted by 23 October, with a final witness list by 27 November.

The timings were agreed with representatives from Lincolnshire Police and Lincolnshire County Council who joined Friday's hybrid hearing remotely, along with Bronson's sister and mother.

At the opening of the inquest in June 2024, coroner Paul Smith heard Bronson had died from dehydration and "appeared to be quite malnourished".

Pre-inquest reviews are an administrative case management hearing to ensure that an inquest is managed effectively, efficiently and openly, according to the Courts and Tribunals Judiciary.

27 December 2023: A social worker "has contact" with Kenneth Battersby and a home visit is arranged

2 January 2024: The social worker arrives at the property but there is no response at the door. She tries to locate Bronson at other addresses and, unable to find him, speaks to her manager and the police

4 January 2024: A second attempt at a home visit is made. Again, there is no response. The social worker informs police

9 January 2024: A third attempt is made and the social worker alerts Battersby's landlady. Entry is gained and the bodies of both father and son are found

15 January 2024: County council notifies the Child Safeguarding Practice Review Panel (CSPRP) of a serious incident that meets the criteria for rapid review

17 January 2024: Council confirms a review is under way and Lincolnshire Police says it has referred itself to the IOPC

20 February 2024: Lincolnshire Safeguarding Children Partnership announces an in-depth independent review supported by the Child Safeguarding Practice Review Panel

6 June 2024: Inquest hears two-year-old Bronson died from dehydration. Hearing is adjourned until December

12 September 2024: IOPC confirms investigation into Lincolnshire Police has found "no indication" of a breach in police professional standards

28 November 2024: Pre-inquest review hears it was still not possible to establish when Bronson died

1 May 2026: A fourth pre-inquest review estimates the inquest will take four weeks and is set for early 2027

25 September 2026: A fifth pre-inquest review takes place. A start date of 22 February 2027 is set for a four-week jury inquest

articles.title: JLR is 'jewel in the crown' of UK economy, says PM Andy Burnham
articles.summary: Burnham insists mass car production still has a future in the UK despite concerns over EU policy.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) and the West Midlands automotive sector as the "jewel in the crown" of the UK economy.

Speaking to BBC Politics West Midlands, Burnham insisted mass car production still had a future in the UK and said the government was working with the EU to ensure new rules did not disadvantage British manufacturers.

JLR suppliers have called for government help to move into aerospace and defence, warning that car production faced a long-term decline.

Burnham said he would take the concerns seriously but that his priority remained helping the automotive industry continue.

"We're so proud of JLR and indeed the whole automotive sector across the West Midlands," Burnham said. "It's the jewel in the crown of the UK economy."

He said that there were "pressures" in the global car market, but added: "We're working hard in relation to Europe to make sure that any changes that come through there don't negatively impact on the British car industry."

The UK is seeking to work with the EU over proposed "Made in Europe" rules which are intended to protect European manufacturers from global competition. Burnham has warned that excluding British companies would damage supply chains.

In an open letter, JLR suppliers said the British automotive supply chain was "in the wrong market", calling for help to move automotive businesses into aerospace and defence.

They warned that JLR's plan to cut 4,000 jobs was the "first visible crack" in a supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs.

JLR has its global headquarters in Coventry and plants in Solihull, Castle Bromwich and Wolverhampton in the West Midlands, and Halewood in Merseyside. Its design centre is in Gaydon, Warwickshire.

Burnham confirmed he was prepared to consider the proposal.

He said: "Those companies that have written, we will take seriously what they've said, as well as supporting the primary interest which is the car industry in the West Midlands."

The government has previously suggested grants, lower energy costs and investment in electric vehicles as measures to support the sector.

"That's the very purpose of the place where we are now, number 10 North. It's all about supporting growth in all parts of the country and we're never going to let industry just go", he added.

He said previous governments had allowed industries in the West Midlands and North West to decline.

"That happened in the 1980s in the West Midlands, and here in the North West where industries that were facing difficulty were just left and the jobs were just allowed to go," he said. "I would never do that."

The prime minister said "supporting industrial transition" was part of his policy of reindustrialisation.

articles.title: Report finds many security deficiencies at Utah university where Charlie Kirk was killed
articles.summary: Charlie Kirk’s political organization insisted he speak outdoors at the Utah university where he was assassinated, despite security concerns from campus offi...
articles.body:
SALT LAKE CITY (AP) — Charlie Kirk's political organization insisted he speak outdoors at the Utah university where he was assassinated , despite security concerns from campus officials who then failed to properly assess dangers including a potential rooftop shooter, according to a report released Friday.

An external review released by Utah Valley University found that the school failed to conduct a formal security assessment, did not create a written event action plan and deferred critical decision-making to Turning Point USA , the Kirk-led organization that scheduled his appearances on college campuses across the U.S.

A charismatic but polarizing figure, Kirk, 31, was killed on Sept. 10, 2025 , by a sniper perched on a rooftop more than 400 feet (122 meters) away, authorities said. The conservative activist had been debating students before a crowd of thousands in an outdoor courtyard surrounded by tall buildings and elevated walkways on the campus in Orem, about 40 miles (64 kilometers) south of Salt Lake City. His appearances often attracted protests, further complicating his security.

Tyler Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in Kirk's killing, a charge that could make him eligible for the death penalty if convicted. Prosecutors say the 23-year-old defendant wrote in a text message about Kirk: "I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can't be negotiated out." No trial date has been set .

Kirk's killing was a watershed moment during a wave of political violence in the United States. President Donald Trump has survived multiple assassination attempts in the past three years, the CEO of UnitedHealthcare was gunned down in 2024 and a Minnesota lawmaker and her husband were killed at their home in 2025.

Utah Valley President Jon Anderson said in a statement that the school has a responsibility to "learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations."

The report echoes complaints made by Kirk's family

Last week, Kirk's family announced a wrongful death notice — a precursor to a possible lawsuit — accusing Utah Valley officials of hastening his death with a string of "reckless decisions."

They included failing to conduct an adequate risk assessment, failing to establish a secure perimeter and failing to have first responders immediately available, which led to Kirk being taken to a hospital in a private vehicle instead of an ambulance.

The family's lawyer, Brett Parkinson, said in a statement that the report reaffirms those allegations. By hosting the event, he said, Utah Valley assumed responsibility for the safety of all in attendance, including Kirk.

"The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU's fatal shortcomings that day."

University officials had suggested other locations for the event

According to the report, which Utah Valley said was done independently by outside consultants, some university officials expressed reservations in an August 2025 meeting with Turning Point about holding the event in an outdoor space surrounded by tall buildings.

The officials suggested multiple other locations, including some that were indoors. But a Turning Point representative insisted that Kirk speak at a campus courtyard because he had been there previously and the organization was familiar with the location. The university ultimately allowed the event to go forward in the courtyard.

"In our assessment, those decisions were consequential," the report said.

Turning Point USA deferred to Parkinson's statement when asked for comment on the findings. The organization and its security team did not respond to several requests to participate in the review, according to the report.

The event location "created significant protective operations considerations," the report said, but the planning process failed to include a documented line-of-sight assessment, pre-event briefing or walk-through with security stakeholders. Nor was there clear coordination with Kirk's private security team and external law enforcement partners, the report said.

An Associated Press review last year found that the campus did not use several public safety practices that have become standard at events around the country. Campus police did not fly a drone to monitor rooftops or coordinate with local law enforcement to secure the event attended by about 3,000 people. There were no bag checks or metal detectors.

The report notes a walk-through didn't happen the day of the event

The report also highlighted a lack of coordination and communication between campus police and Kirk's private security in the days leading up to the event.

In foregoing a day-of walk-through and pre-event briefing, they missed opportunities to go over roles, assess staffing and equipment, add resources such as drones, and address any concerns or threats, the report said.

The university's police chief sent a text message asking Turning Point's security supervisor to meet at the event location a few hours beforehand, but no meeting ever happened, the report said.

Utah Valley University says it is making key changes

The report makes nearly 150 recommendations, including hiring a police sergeant to focus on campus events and creating clear criteria for when events must be moved indoors or to more controllable venues.

"This requires humility, an honest examination of our policies and practices, and a commitment to act on what we learn," said Anderson, who took over as university president last month. He added that the university has made "meaningful progress in strengthening campus safety over the past year."

That includes hiring a chief public safety officer to coordinate with emergency response agencies and hiring more campus police officers . At the time of the shooting, the university had just 13 sworn officers, which the report said was not sufficient for Utah Valley's size and the types of events held on the campus. It's the state's largest university, with about 50,000 students on a sprawling campus in Orem, beneath the Wasatch Mountains.

Sisak reported from New York. Associated Press reporter Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed.

articles.title: End employment-based Green Card, prioritize English proficiency: Republican Senator brings new America First bill
articles.summary: Amid several sweeping changes to the US immigration rules, Republican Senator Tommy Tuberville has introduced new legislation seeking to end Green Card
articles.body: Amid several sweeping changes to the US immigration rules, Republican Senator Tommy Tuberville has introduced new legislation seeking to end Green Card lottery and employment-based Green Cards. This is just legislation and many such pieces of legislation are proposed regularly by lawmakers, which never see the light of day.The Americans First Immigration Act, introduced by the Alabama Republican on September 24, would require employers seeking to hire foreign workers to first recruit US workers and certify that the foreign hire would not displace an American worker. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.What happens to employment-based Green cards?Under the proposal, the existing employment-based immigrant visa categories would be replaced with a points-based programme. Applicants would earn points for factors including education, English-language proficiency, high-paying US job offers, military service and extraordinary achievement.The legislation intends to move away from the current employment-based Green Card structure and instead assess applicants according to a set of merit-based criteria.The bill also proposes a new employer-attestation system. Employers would have to show that they made good-faith efforts to recruit US workers and offered the position to a US worker who was equally or better qualified. They would also have to attest that they had not laid off a US worker from an essentially equivalent job during the specified period before hiring the foreign worker.Employers that violate the requirements could face civil penalties. The bill provides for penalties of up to $5,000 for certain violations, $25,000 for each willful violation and $50,000 when a willful violation results in a US worker being laid off. A pattern or practice of noncompliance could also trigger criminal penalties.Green Card lottery would endOne of the bill's major proposals is the elimination of the Diversity Immigrant Visa programme, commonly known as the Green Card lottery. The program currently makes a limited number of immigrant visas available through a lottery to people from countries with historically lower levels of immigration to the US.Tuberville's bill would replace that system with a merit-based approach. His office said the proposal would reward factors such as skills, education, English proficiency and high-value job offers rather than selection by lottery.Family immigration would be sharply narrowedUnder the proposal, family-sponsored immigration would be limited to the immediate or "nuclear" family, specifically spouses and minor children. This would eliminate several existing categories through which US citizens and lawful permanent residents can sponsor other relatives.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Omar brings J&K statehood resolution to assembly, autonomy mention sparks BJP furore
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: Chief minister Omar Abdullah brought Friday an assembly resolution seeking restoration of full statehood for J&K, but an autonomy reference
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Chief minister Omar Abdullah brought Friday an assembly resolution seeking restoration of full statehood for J&K, but an autonomy reference ignited a BJP backlash, with its members ripping up copies amid anti-national chants directed at the governing National Conference (NC).The contentious reference came as the document cited an autonomy resolution passed by the assembly in June 2000 when J&K was a state.For nearly two years, Omar has called on the Centre to restore statehood. Soon after taking office, his cabinet passed a resolution to this effect. NC legislators argued that the Centre’s lack of movement forced the party to bring the resolution to the assembly.Omar echoed the sentiment, saying it seems the cabinet was not seen as the sole voice of the people by the Centre, while the legislature represents a broader political spectrum as it includes parties outside govt. “Statehood is not about govt or my family. It is about J&K. That is why we brought it to the House so that a united voice can go to the Centre,” the CM said.As BJP legislators shouted slogans and tore copies, members of NC ally Congress supported the resolution and confronted rivals. CPM, Peoples Conference and PDP also backed the resolution.Leader of opposition, BJP’s Sunil Sharma, accused Omar of trying to “smuggle in” the 2000 autonomy move dressed up as a “statehood restoration resolution”. He recalled that then PM Atal Bihari Vajpayee’s govt had rejected the 2000 resolution and asserted that BJP will not tolerate its revival now. Angered by this, some NC legislators displayed banners reading “we want autonomy of J&K be restored.” Others called for restoration of Article 370.Omar argued that statehood was a promise made by the Centre and reaffirmed by PM Narendra Modi at an event where Sharma was present. “Delimitation was carried out. Elections were held (in 2024). People voted without any coercion. But the third step of the promise, restoration of statehood, was not fulfilled,” Omar said, citing assurances given by the Centre in Parliament and Supreme Court.Explaining the reference to previous resolutions, the CM said the aim was to convey that the House continued to stand by all past decisions. “Our friends shouldn’t say that we have given up on them. Those resolutions remain in place. This resolution neither replaces nor ignores them. It is an addition to them,” the CM said. The expression “friends” was seen as an allusion to PDP.Speaking to reporters later, Omar rejected BJP’s charges and asked “how demanding statehood can be anti-national”. The CM has been under pressure for several months now, accused by rivals of dropping demands to restore Article 370 and demanding statehood only. articles.title: In a first, waste plastic mixed with bitumen in pilot test section of NH-44
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In a first for the road sector, govt has used waste plastic as a wet mix with bitumen to lay a bituminous highway stretch, a move that is
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a first for the road sector, govt has used waste plastic as a wet mix with bitumen to lay a bituminous highway stretch, a move that is likely to reduce imports of the key construction material while addressing the growing problem of plastic waste.On Thursday, a pilot test section was laid on the main carriageway of NH-44 in Jhansi. Officials associated with the pilot said the technology has potential to reduce conventional bitumen consumption by around 4%, lowering demand for a material that India largely imports to meet domestic requirements. They added that the modified bitumen could cost around 20% less than conventional bitumen.The waste plastic wet-process technology for producing premium-quality Waste Plastic Modified Bitumen (W-PMB 76-10) has been developed by IIT (BHU), Varanasi, under a research programme funded by the ministry of road transport and highways. The performance of the pilot stretch will be monitored by IIT (BHU) to assess its long-term engineering performance and field suitability, officials said.India generates around 25,000 tonne of plastic waste every day. Until now, waste plastic has been used in road construction only as a dry mix with aggregates while laying the bituminous layer. The new method mixes processed waste plastic directly with bitumen before it is laid, making it the first such pilot on a national highway.Officials said the technology offers multiple benefits, including the value-added reuse of waste plastic through a scientifically controlled process and improved rut resistance of bituminous mixes under high ambient temperatures and heavy axle loads.The technology has also recently been granted a patent. The low-density polyethylene (LDPE) used in the process — a soft, flexible and lightweight thermoplastic made from petroleum — includes discarded irrigation pipes, waste files and plastic folders. The material has been processed with the support of local recyclers and MSMEs, creating an opportunity to integrate local waste recycling with infrastructure development.“Laboratory evaluations have shown that LDPE-modified bitumen provides better resistance to moisture damage and greater resistance to rutting at high temperatures. The modified binder increases the stiffness and high-temperature performance of asphalt, helping pavements withstand permanent deformation under heavy traffic loads and extreme temperatures,” an official said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: A Finnish metal detectorist has uncovered what is believed to be the country's largest known Viking Age silver coin hoard after finding thousands of
articles.body: A Finnish metal detectorist has uncovered what is believed to be the country's largest known Viking Age silver coin hoard after finding thousands of ancient coins near the village centre of Sysmä. Kalle Lappinen discovered the hoard on September 3, 2026, and reported the find to authorities, allowing archaeologists from Lahti Museums to begin recovering the material the following day. The discovery contains thousands of silver coins weighing about 4.5 kilograms, along with other silver objects. What makes the find particularly unusual is that the treasure was divided between two birch-bark containers buried about 12 metres, or 39 feet, apart. The hoard is preliminarily dated to around AD 1000 to 1050.Metal detector leads to thousands of Viking Age silver coinsLappinen was searching near Sysmä when his metal detector led him to the buried material. The discovery soon revealed an unusually large concentration of silver coins, far exceeding the scale of most Late Iron Age hoards previously found in the area. Archaeologists from Lahti Museums began recovering the objects on September 4. The coins and other material were carefully removed for conservation and examination, with archaeologist Esko Tikkala overseeing the recovery. The recovered coins weigh approximately 4.5 kilograms, or nearly 10 pounds. Alongside the coins, archaeologists found hack silver, a silver bracelet, a mount and a bead, adding to the archaeological significance of the discovery.Two birch-bark containers found 39 feet apartThe silver was not hidden in one single cache. Instead, the treasure had been divided between two deposits located roughly 12 metres, or 39 feet, apart. Both deposits were placed in birch-bark containers and buried about 45 centimetres underground among stones. The unusual arrangement has led Frida Ehrnsten, keeper of the numismatic collections at the National Museum of Finland, to describe the discovery as a kind of "double hoard". The two deposits provide an unusual glimpse into how valuable possessions could be concealed during the Late Iron Age. Why the silver was divided into two locations, however, remains unknown.Hoard contains coins from across Europe and beyondThe coins reveal how widely silver circulated during the period. Among the discoveries are coins associated with areas corresponding to modern-day Sweden, Britain and Germany, as well as Islamic dirhams originating from regions corresponding to present-day Turkey and Iran. The mixture points to extensive connections between the region around Sysmä and wider trading networks. Researchers can use the coins' designs, inscriptions and dates to establish where they were produced and trace the movement of silver into Finland. The find therefore offers more than evidence of a large personal fortune. It could provide new information about trade, wealth and economic connections across northern Europe around 1,000 years ago.Hoard dates to around AD 1000 to 1050The hoard is currently dated to approximately AD 1000 to 1050, placing it within the period known as the Viking Age. Researchers are continuing to clean and examine the coins, which will allow them to establish more precise dates for individual pieces. The term Viking Age refers to the broader historical period and does not establish that the people living in Finland at the time were Vikings. The range of coins also reflects the complex movement of silver during this period, when precious metal could travel considerable distances through trade and other forms of exchange.Why the treasure was buried remains a mysteryThe person who accumulated the silver and buried it has never been identified. Tikkala has suggested that the hoard could have belonged to a merchant who temporarily buried part of his wealth for safekeeping and planned to retrieve it later. Another possibility is that a wealthy local resident hid the silver because of the threat of conflict or an enemy attack. The treasure's owner never returned, leaving the reason for its burial unknown. The decision to divide the silver between two deposits adds another unanswered question to the discovery.Sysmä was an important Late Iron Age hubThe hoard is also shedding light on the history of Sysmä itself. Although the area may appear relatively modest today, archaeological evidence suggests it was a significant location during the Late Iron Age. Tikkala said the discovery provides further evidence that Sysmä was an important hub with trade connections extending in several directions. The presence of silver from Scandinavia, Britain, Germany and regions farther east supports the picture of a community connected to wider networks. The newly discovered hoard could therefore help researchers understand the role that Sysmä played in the movement of silver and other goods.Previous Finnish record had about 1,700 coinsThe scale of the discovery becomes clearer when compared with Finland's previous largest known Viking Age coin hoard. That hoard was discovered in Nousiainen in 1895 and contained approximately 1,700 coins. The Sysmä discovery has surpassed that record, with thousands of coins recovered so far. Some reports have estimated that the new hoard contains more than 4,000 coins, although researchers are still cleaning, separating and cataloguing the material to establish the final count. The Sysmä discovery is already substantially larger than the previous record in terms of recovered coins and silver, making it an important addition to Finland's archaeological record.Researchers continue to study the ancient fortuneThe investigation is now focused on identifying and documenting the individual coins and other objects. Researchers will examine their dates, origins and inscriptions while studying the birch-bark containers and the circumstances in which the two deposits were buried. The work could reveal when the silver was accumulated, how it reached Sysmä and what the different groups of coins say about trade networks of the period. For now, the discovery has left archaeologists with a remarkable archaeological puzzle. Thousands of pieces of silver, accumulated from places stretching across Europe and beyond, were hidden in two containers just 39 feet apart and remained underground for roughly 1,000 years before a metal detectorist uncovered them.You use AI every day. articles.title: Brewery that offered free beer when Trump dies faces possible closure after state revokes alcohol permits
articles.summary: Minocqua Brewing Co.'s Madison taproom faces likely closure by year's end after Wisconsin officials revoked its alcohol permits over alleged violations.
articles.body: The owner of Minocqua Brewing Co. said Monday that the Madison taproom in Wisconsin will likely shut down by the end of the year after state officials revoked the company’s alcohol permits. Channel 3000 reported that Minocqua Brewing Co. owner Kirk Bangstad said the Madison taproom is likely to shut down as the business continues fighting the state’s decision. The brewery has become known for its outspoken messaging against President Donald Trump. WISCONSIN BREWERY THAT OFFERED 'FREE BEER' WHEN TRUMP DIES SAYS ALCOHOL PERMIT REVOKED The Wisconsin Department of Revenue (DOR) revoked brewing permits for the company’s Minocqua and Madison locations after alleging violations involving beer transported from Illinois without the required permits and tax payments. The brewery has disputed the state’s action and accused officials of targeting it because of its political views. The department told Fox News Digital in a statement Thursday that there is a hearing on the company's appeal on Nov. 18, and that the revocation does not take effect until appeals are done, adding that the "DOR is dedicated to fair and consistent enforcement of alcohol beverage regulations in Wisconsin and takes action when the laws are not followed, as occurred here." Bangstad’s breweries have made headlines for offering free beer if President Trump dies. On Jan. 22, the Minocqua Brewing Company appeared to suggest it would give free beer to patrons if Trump was killed, and while not explicitly using his name, posted on Facebook, "Free beer, all day long the day he dies." 'FREE BEER' FOR TRUMP DEATH DEM ACTIVIST RUNNING FOR WISCONSIN GOV: 'I WILL WIN' IF THEY SILENCE ME "Show us this post when it happens in a few months and we’ll make good on that promise," the post continued. The post was updated to say, "We meant the Madison Taproom because that’s open all year, if he dies in the summer, then it’s gonna be the Minocqua Taproom." In reply to comment on the post, the company also did not refer to Trump by name but said the message referred to a high-profile figure when asked whether the timeline for the deal could be moved up earlier. After the April shooting at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner where Trump was present, the company wrote on Facebook, "Well, we almost got #freebeerday." KENTUCKY GOVERNOR SAYS HE RECEIVED 2 CALLS FROM AGENCIES INDICATING MCCONNELL HAD 'PASSED' The brewery also offered half-price beer when Sen. Mitch McConnell dies. "When they announce that McConnell’s Faustian dance has finally ended, we’re gonna start serving our beer at ‘half price,’ because we promised #halfpricebeerday on the day they unplug the ventilator," the brewery said in an Instagram post. McConnell, who is 84, was absent from the Senate for months after being hospitalized for a fall in his home earlier this year. The Kentucky Republican returned to the Senate last week ahead of key votes. Bangstad, who owns the brewery, is also the founder of the Minocqua Brewing Company SuperPAC, which "aims to remove Republican federal and state elected officials who perpetuated the election lies that caused the Insurrection of January 6, 2021, and whose downplaying of the seriousness of COVID-19 caused so many unnecessary deaths in our country," according to the brewery’s website. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Reached for comment by Fox News Digital, the brewery made disparaging remarks about Trump and again noted that it will host a "#freebeerday" when the president passes. "Reminder, however, no red hats allowed," the brewery added.

articles.title: What is kratom, the 'gas station heroin' alarming officials in the US
articles.summary: Kratom, found during an investigation into the deaths of two college students, has been sold in the US for around a decade.
articles.body:
Jeffrey Deaver, a 58-year-old retired timber cutter in the state of Washington, has taken kratom for four years to help with severe chronic hip and knee pain.

He discovered the herbal product when he couldn't find relief from doctors and while waiting for surgeries. Scared at first, he "started small", but then took more until his pain went away.

"It was like a miracle," Deaver said. "I could sleep. I could function.

"I just don't know what I'd do without it."

Kratom - an herb with opioid-like effects - has grown in popularity in the US over the last decade, and is typically purchased over-the-counter and consumed in pill or liquid form.

This week, investigators found packaged kratom in the possession of two deceased University of Mississippi students. Although their deaths were not attributed to kratom, officials are now issuing warnings about its consumption.

For years, anti-kratom advocates have pushed for bans, and in some countries, like the UK, it's illegal. But Kratom is not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration and is legal in some states, including Mississippi.

Kratom is a tree that is native to Southeast Asia in countries like Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia.

It's been used for centuries for its stimulant properties, grounded and consumed similar to tea.

As its popularity spread around the globe, it entered the US market as a supplement around 2016.

"That's really where the problems began," said Dr Shane Speights, dean of the New York Institute of Technology College of Osteopathic Medicine at Arkansas State University.

In the US kratom is mostly sold in highly concentrated forms either via pill, powder or liquid, Speights said.

It's also widely available - found everywhere from convenience stores and petrol stations to vape shops.

Also, because of the supplement classification, kratom products are not federally regulated.

"There's no way to know exactly what you're getting," Speight said. "You could go and create something in your basement, market it as a supplement, and nobody's really going to check and see what's in it."

Kratom is often marketed as a safe, natural herbal supplement that helps with pain management, anxiety and depression.

In lower doses, its stimulant properties create a "caffeine-kind of buzz", Speights explained.

Because of its opioid-like effects, it has also been used with the goal of curbing addictions to actual opioids like fentanyl.

Those properties stem from the way the plant's compounds - like 7-Hydroxymitragynine - activate various hormones, including dopamine.

What are the effects and how dangerous is it?

"It's almost like taking a narcotic," Speights said. "At higher doses, it can create more euphoria and give you more of a general high."

The higher doses also pose greater risk for adverse side effects.

That includes central nervous system (CNS) depression - which is "where the deaths come in," Speights said.

CNS can result in cardiovascular collapse and loss of breathing.

Withdrawal symptoms and addiction are also risks, said Jana Wu, director of clinical integration at the addiction treatment centre Mountainside.

"It affects marriages, relationships," she said. "I've seen people lose jobs, spend thousands of dollars a month on it."

Because it's easy to develop a high tolerance to the herb, users may need to take an increasing amount to achieve the same effect over time.

"I've worked with people that were taking like up to 20 pills a day," Wu said.

Experts told the BBC that the biggest dangers come from the fact that kratom is not federally regulated.

"Is there a safe dose?" Speights said. "My answer is going to be no because - I'm going to go back to this - we don't know what's in it."

Kratom is banned in 11 states: Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Massachusetts, North Dakota, Tennessee, Vermont and Wisconsin.

Massachusetts was the last state to make it illegal, issuing a temporary emergency order in August.

Ten years earlier, the US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) had moved to classify kratom as a Schedule 1, the most dangerous level for drugs, calling it "an imminent hazard to public safety".

But the effort failed a few months later, after the justice department said it received "numerous comments from members of the public challenging" the attempt.

That leaves states to take action, like Arizona, which recently sued a company selling kratom beverage products.

Groups opposed to kratom want states to do more, saying "gas-station drugs are poisoning our communities".

Pro-kratom groups like the American Kratom Association are pushing for bans against synthetics "posing as natural kratom".

Internationally, kratom is banned in the UK. In Europe, the laws vary by country.

In Malaysia, where the kratom tree is native, consumption and sale are banned under the Poisons Act of 1952.

articles.title: In 2024, 75-year-old Iowa farmer Evie Haupt said three wind turbines on her 160 acres were bringing in about $35,000 a year while using under 3 acres and had helped reduce $350,000 in farm debt to $67,000
articles.summary: On a 160-acre farm in central Iowa, three tall wind turbines quietly rise above the fields.
articles.body: On a 160-acre farm in central Iowa, three tall wind turbines quietly rise above the fields. Each turbine uses less than an acre of land, but together they provide an annual income that has changed the financial future of 75-year-old farmer Evie Haupt. According to a CBS News report by Janet Shamlian and Alicia Hastey, Haupt earns about $35,000 each year by leasing part of her land for the wind turbines. The income rises with inflation and has helped her pay down a $350,000 farm debt left after her husband died a decade ago. Her remaining debt is now $67,000. For many family farms across the United States, extra sources of income have become important lifelines. The U.S. Department of Agriculture expects farm profits to fall by 25 per cent, as farmers face higher costs, changing crop prices and unpredictable weather. Adding wind power to traditional farming can provide steady income and help protect farmers from financial shocks.A financial lifeline for rural landownersFarm debt can force families to make difficult choices, including selling land that has been passed down through generations. Haupt faced a major financial challenge after her husband died, leaving behind hundreds of thousands of dollars in farm debt. Payments from the wind turbines gave her a steady source of money that could go toward those loans. Each turbine uses less than an acre, so Haupt can still farm most of her 160 acres. This gives her two sources of income from the same land, while using only a small part of the property for the turbines. The payments can also rise over time because the contracts include inflation adjustments. This helps protect landowners as prices and other costs change. For Haupt, the result has been major. She has paid off more than 80 per cent of her farm debt while keeping the land in use.The explosive expansion of Iowa wind powerIowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Iowa had only a few hundred wind turbines 20 years ago. Today, it has more than 6,000, producing about 60 per cent of the state's energy. Across the United States, more than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Federal energy officials also say current U.S. wind power cuts carbon emissions by an amount equal to taking 73 million passenger vehicles off the road. Attorney Kathy Law, who grew up on a farm and married a farmer, has helped place nearly half of Iowa's wind turbines. Her work in energy law grew from her own family's experience with farming. Law wanted to study law while she was in high school, but the severe farm crisis of the 1980s kept her home to help with the family farm. She later went to law school in her forties. She graduated on the same day her son finished high school and later served as president of the Iowa Wind Energy Association for three years. "From my farm background, I think I can talk their talk and have conversations with landowners that are interested in having wind turbines on their property," Law told CBS News.Addressing local pushback and debateThe rapid growth of wind power in rural communities has also brought opposition in some counties. Local critics say wind turbines can change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats. Law believes landowners should be able to decide what happens on their property. "Nobody's requiring them to put that on their farms or on their land," Law said during her interview with CBS News. "We want to be able to put turbines on our land and receive those benefits." Haupt has a similar view of the changes to her farm. While she remains attached to traditional farming, she sees clean energy as an important step for rural communities. "I look at it as progress," Haupt told CBS News. "I think we can't stand in the way of progress." For Haupt, giving up a very small part of her land to produce electricity makes sense for her finances and for the wider community. "I need to give up one or two acres of my land so that I can generate a commodity that we all use every day, and we all want to use more of it every day," Haupt said. "So I'm happy to be able to be a part of that generation."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Michigan CEO who posted AI photo of family members wearing ‘Lake America’ sweatshirts loses job; she says it was just for fun, not a political message
articles.summary: A Michigan credit union CEO whose AI-generated photograph of her family wearing “Lake America” sweatshirts went viral during a trip to Canada is no longer
articles.body: A Michigan credit union CEO whose AI-generated photograph of her family wearing “Lake America” sweatshirts went viral during a trip to Canada is no longer with the organization. Michigan borders Canada and the company did not risk upsetting the neighbor.Jane Smith, former CEO of Family First Credit Union in Saginaw, Michigan, ceased to be an employee of the credit union with immediate effect, according to a statement issued by the organization. Chief operating officer Jason Acosta has been appointed interim CEO.The credit union did not specify whether Smith resigned or was dismissed, nor did it explicitly say that the AI-generated image was the reason for her departure. However, the announcement came days after the photograph triggered widespread backlash in Canada.What was in the AI-generated photo?Smith and three members of her family had travelled to Halifax, Nova Scotia, for a 10-day holiday beginning September 11.Before the trip, the family discussed President Donald Trump's move to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”. Smith later said they took a family photograph at Detroit Metropolitan Airport and used ChatGPT to digitally add matching “Lake America” sweatshirts to the image.Smith posted the altered photograph on her private Facebook account with an indication that it had been generated using AI. The caption read: “Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will,” followed by “lol lol.”Smith said the photograph was intended as a joke and was not meant to make a political statement.“We weren't trying to make a political statement,” she told ABC12 News, explaining that the family was “kind of poking fun” at the controversy surrounding the proposed name change.Smith's sister then posted the same photograph without the AI label. It quickly spread online, with many people apparently interpreting the image as a genuine photograph of an American family wearing the sweatshirts while visiting Canada.Smith said that the family had never actually owned or worn the sweatshirts.“We never had actual sweatshirts. We never wore sweatshirts,” she said.Backlash and apologyThe photograph generated an angry response in Canada, where the proposed renaming of Lake Ontario has been politically sensitive.Smith later apologized for posting the image and acknowledged that creating and sharing it had been a mistake. She also warned about the potential for AI-generated images to be mistaken for real photographs.“I think the AI can be dangerous in the fact that it can make people think something's real that's not,” she said.Smith also said that her family cut short its Canadian trip after she received death threats following the controversy.Credit union distanced from the postFamily First Credit Union's board had previously criticised the photograph, saying it did not reflect the organisation's values. The controversy involved Smith acting in a personal capacity while travelling with her family, rather than making the post as an official representative of the credit union. After announcing Smith's departure, Family First said: “We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community.”The Lake America controversyThe photograph emerged amid a broader dispute over Trump's decision to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” in US federal usage.The lake borders both the United States and Canada, and the proposed name change has drawn opposition in Canada. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canadians will continue to call it Lake Ontario. Meanwhile, three US lawmakers have introduced legislation seeking to prevent the renaming.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
