articles.title: Carville says the GOP is better than Democrats at one key skill the 2028 Dem nominee will need
articles.summary: James Carville says Democrats lack a consistent negative and positive narrative, warning the party's 2028 nominee must master political messaging to win.
articles.body: Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville said Republicans are better at pushing positive and negative narratives than Democrats on Thursday and warned his party that its 2028 nominee will need that skill to win. Carville has frequently condemned the Trump administration, predicting that 2026 will be a year of landmark victories for the Democratic Party. He has suggested multiple times that President Donald Trump, after presumably losing political power in the midterms, may resign from office early and be pardoned by Vice President JD Vance after Vance becomes president. One listener, however, contacted Carville and his co-host Al Hunt on their "Politics War Room" podcast, juxtaposing how Republicans and Democrats talk about each other. "He wants to know why the Republicans are so much better than the Democrats at creating boogeymen," Hunt summarized. "Republicans will paint all Democrats with a socialist brush, yet Democrats can’t seem to do the same thing when it comes to racism, antisemitism or corruption, despite the fact that all three are prevalent among Republican members of Congress." 100 DAYS UNTIL MIDTERMS AND DEMOCRATS ARE WINNING BECAUSE THEY ACTUALLY HAVE A MESSAGE "The gist of the question is Republicans are very good at painting Democrats as boogeymen, socialists, communists, all that kind of stuff," Hunt continued. "But the Democrats don’t do as good a job, Rob worries, about painting Republicans with their racism, antisemitism, etc." Carville argued that the Republicans are doing so badly they may not even need the Democrats to condemn them. "First of all, it is a good question," Carville replied. "Secondly, what’s happened now is they’re painting themselves that way, OK? They’re going down not because of Democratic messaging, not because of a relentless offense by the Democrats that, you know, points out their foibles. They’re going down because the public sees it, and they don’t need that. A Democratic intervention right now is not called for." Carville said that the Democratic nominee will need to master this skill to win in 2028. "The gist of the question from our listener is totally correct. And for whatever reasons, Ben [sic], I think it’s because we’re more of a coalition. Not only do we not have a consistent negative story to tell about the other party, we don’t have a consistent positive story to tell about ourselves," he said. "Hope and pray that in 2028 we have a really skilled candidate that’s able to do that." "But that is a fact of American politics," he added. "We’re not as good as they are at the negative, and we’re not as good as they are at a positive." SOCIALISTS ARE HELPING GOP CAMPAIGNS HEADING INTO NOVEMBER Mary Marslender, a former senior advisor to Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., and a former Trump appointee who is now a Republican consultant, said there is a disparity in how well each side uses that rhetoric against the other. "It isn’t even close, and it isn’t the disparity Carville thinks it is," she told Fox News Digital. "When Republicans label Democrats as socialists, it’s not just empty rhetoric; it’s grounded in how many Democrats describe themselves. Recent polling found that 59 percent of Democrats identify as supporters of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)." "The DSA has openly advocated for policies such as court-packing, sweeping changes to financial institutions, the abolition of capitalism, open borders, eliminating prisons and the Senate, and expanding administrative power. The Democratic Party has embraced socialism, and there seems to be no turning back," Marslender continued. However, she disagreed with Carville's comment that Republicans have already destroyed their own reputation without Democratic help. "Carville’s claim is more political spin than reality," Marslender said. "If Republicans had truly destroyed their own credibility, Democrats would not need Carville’s advice to ‘sit this one out.’ In fact, Carville reveals the Democratic Party’s real problem: they lack both a compelling message and a strong messenger, and are now hoping for a ‘really skilled candidate in 2028.’" "A party that has watched the Trump administration deliver on border security, energy independence, and prioritizing American workers cannot credibly claim that Republicans have already undermined themselves," she continued. "If Republicans were as self-destructive as Carville claims, Democrats wouldn’t be waiting for a future savior; they would already be capitalizing on Republicans’ so-called failures. Carville’s argument underscores that Democrats still recognize weaknesses in their own positioning and strategy." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Julian Epstein, an attorney, Democratic consultant and former Democratic chief counsel for the House Judiciary Committee, said some of Carville's comments were "delusion." "Some of this is progressive delusion," he said. "For the last decade, Democrats, in non-stop fashion, have sought to commodify rage by calling Trump a fascist, deriding Trump’s attempt to stop a Nazi movement in the Mideast, and blaming him for a cost-of-living crisis that Democrats mostly authored under Biden’s 20% cumulative inflation. Most of what Democrats do today is name-calling." "Democrats failure to tell a ‘positive story’ is not a communications problem, it’s a philosophy problem," Epstein added. "It dismays many of us centrists, but the left’s program today is almost entirely identity grievance and tax-and-spend redistributionist big government, which appeals to, at most, 25% of voters — about the same low number of voters that actually identify as Democrats today." "Democrats have forgotten how to build," he continued. "They have forgotten that the story of America is one of innovation, invention and discovery, not resentment and big government bureaucracies." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "At the same time, it is also true that the GOP is squandering its 2024 mandate," Epstein added. "Its tripping over itself with badly designed tariffs, has failed to show in a forward-looking manner that building new housing and increasing competition in health insurance can cure a lot of the affordability problem, and has failed to explain that we are fighting a KKK-like ideology in the Mideast. Unlike the Democrats’ philosophy problem, the GOP has a yawning communications’ problem."

articles.title: Black woman found hanging from tree was dead before body was 'staged', US media reports
articles.summary: Tasia Fortune's body was found hanging from a tree on the grounds of an abandoned home in Jackson in August.
articles.body:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

Police in the US state of Mississippi have said that they believe a black woman was already dead before her body was "staged" and placed hanging in a tree, the Associated Press reports.

The disclosure was made in court by a detective on Friday, who also said they believed Tasia Fortune had been killed in a dispute related to drugs, US media reported.

The 29-year-old's body was found hanging from a tree on the grounds of an abandoned home in Jackson in August.

The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city, due to the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. After weeks of speculation and demands for information, police made multiple arrests.

The BBC has contacted the court, the medical examiner's office and Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey.

In a statement to the BBC on Friday, Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney said "Our language has been consistent...Ms Fortune was found in a hanging position. We have not released any information contrary to that statement."

Brackney did not immediately respond to additional questions about the detective's disclosure in court.

Officials have not stated the exact cause of death or shared why they believe the hanging was staged.

The medical examiner confirmed earlier this month that Fortune's cause of death was homicide and said there would be a murder charge.

Jarques Ratliff, 51, was arrested and pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody in without bond.

A second person, Earnest Lloyd Jr, 25, was arrested in the case this week, while a third was reportedly being sought by authorities.

The 29-year-old's death is one of several cases in recent years that has prompted lawmakers to call on the justice department and the FBI to investigate all hanging deaths of black people in the country.

Representative Ayanna Pressley, Democrat of Massachusetts, cites at least 10 documented incidents in her September letter to Congress , which contained over 50 signatures from US lawmakers.

The most recent incident happened in Prince George's County, a majority-black suburb near Washington DC, on Sunday. It has been ruled a suicide.

articles.title: 'Transparency' call over £68m Dumfries flood scheme information
articles.summary: The council response to Mike Sutherland over the Dumfries project was deemed "entirely unacceptable".
articles.body:
The man behind the freedom of information (FOI) requests where a council response was found to be "entirely unacceptable" has called for someone to be held to account.

Mike Sutherland said he believed there had been a "catalogue of errors" in the handling of the £68m Whitesands flood protection scheme in Dumfries.

The Scottish Information Commissioner (SIC) recently ruled that Dumfries and Galloway Council had "failed at the most basic level" in its response to his requests about the project.

The council said it was considering the findings and would respond within the timescales set out.

Council's flood scheme request approach 'entirely unacceptable'

The street that has flooded more than 200 times

Opponents say it is too costly, spoils the view and costs car parking spaces.

Those in favour argue it will provide defences to an area which has flooded hundreds of times and also help with its regeneration.

Sutherland believes the Local Government (Scotland) Act 1973 required the council to seek court approval to use common good land.

After an attempt to fund a challenge through the courts raised only a fraction of the funding required, the former council worker from Lockerbie turned to FOIs to raise his concerns about the project.

He asked for information about the use of common good land - owned by the council for the benefit of the community - and whether it had petitioned the courts for a change of use.

The response from the local authority was severely criticised by Scottish Information Commissioner David Hamilton.

Sutherland said that made him feel vindicated in his persistence to get answers about a scheme "hated by many people".

"I've asked them a few more testing questions which they've been very furtive about indeed," he said.

"They're quick enough in making other people accountable - what about their accountability?

"They're going to try and avoid answering all the same - because they want this project as far down the line as possible," he said.

Sutherland said he accepted that the project would go ahead but he still wanted to pursue answers.

"They have no hesitation whatsoever in holding other people to account when they slip up just once," he said.

"They've made a catalogue of errors here over a £68m project that a lot of people do not want."

He said he would not stop until the council was forced to "reveal all they must reveal".

His call received support from MSP Craig Hoy this week.

"There are important questions that Dumfries and Galloway Council must now address," he told the Scottish Parliament.

"It must clearly and willingly explain the legal position surrounding the use of common good land that is affected by the project and show that the proper processes have been pursued at all stages."

He said he would be meeting the council chief executive to ask the council to answer questions about the scheme "fully, openly and transparently".

The council said it was still examining the findings on its FOI responses which were issued a week ago.

"We are currently considering the SIC's decisions and the requirements set out in them," it said.

"We will fully consider and respond within the timescales set out.

"It would be inappropriate to comment further until we have had an opportunity to review the decisions in detail."

articles.title: Katherine Jenkins says paper said it would 'trash her' in early career
articles.summary: The classical star says she was "left staggered" by questions she was asked as a young woman in music.
articles.body:
Katherine Jenkins has reflected on the "crazy" questions she was asked by the press as a young classical singer.

The mezzo-soprano, who has had 14 number one albums, is about to start a tour marking 25 years as one of the world's most successful classical singers.

Jenkins, 46, from Neath, said she had "found her own voice" and learnt to take control of her career over the years, adding that she was often staggered by the things journalists would say to her.

"I would often get asked 'who's looking after your children?' That's crazy. You wouldn't get tenors asked that question," she told BBC Radio Wales .

She recalled being at the Classical Brit Awards early in her career and being told by one journalist that their newspaper loved her, but would have to "trash her" sooner or later.

"There were loads of fake stories I read about myself ordering crazy meals and bonkers demands, and you just think, 'wow, I'd never say that'. But it's something you learn to navigate," she added.

"It takes a lot of hard work and practice to be good at what you do in any field," said Jenkins.

"And when it comes to talking about women, unfortunately, hard work and ambition seems to equal a negative."

She has recently developed a gin brand which is made in Wales and sold around the world, but said people often assumed she was just the face brought into to front it, rather than the entrepreneur behind it.

A quarter of a decade into her career, Jenkins said she had "remained the same person" thanks to her close-knit family and childhood friends who keep her grounded.

She credits her late father, who died when she was 15, who gave her a "quiet confidence", often telling her "I believe in you".

"He was a house husband, which is quite forward thinking for back then. He was picking me up from school, making dinner, taking me to singing lessons or choir practice," said Jenkins.

"There are certain moments when I think 'oh my gosh, my dad would love this'. But I do think he's with me."

There have been many career highlights for Jenkins over the decades, including performing for British troops in Afghanistan, which she described as "emotional" and which led to a long standing relationship with the forces.

Another highlight was recording a classical version of the Dolly Parton hit I Will Always Love You.

Jenkins said she wrote to Parton to ask for her permission to record the song, adding that Parton approved of her version.

"I think I'm the first to sing it in a foreign language which is so amazing to get to do that.

"I got to meet her. She was as charming and funny as you would imagine. I got to see her backstage at the O2 and she said lovely things about it, she was very complimentary, she loved it."

Looking forward the next 25 years, Jenkins said she had her sights on the film industry.

"I think the dream would be to voice an animated character. I think that would be really fun," she said.

articles.title: Michigan’s Brooklyn Dam removed after 85 years; $2 million project transforms 21-acre, 4-to-8-foot-deep River Raisin waterway into faster-flowing stream; five years of planning and construction
articles.summary: For generations, the River Raisin in Brooklyn, Michigan, was a familiar part of everyday life.
articles.body: For generations, the River Raisin in Brooklyn, Michigan, was a familiar part of everyday life. Children skated across its frozen surface in winter, boats moved through it in summer and residents watched sunsets reflected on the water. Today, that landscape looks dramatically different.After nearly five years of planning, public meetings and construction, water once held behind the Brooklyn Dam has been diverted into a newly shaped river channel, leaving what was once a tall, slow-moving stretch of water as a shallower, faster-flowing stream.The project, which cost about $2 million and was funded through a combination of state and federal grants, is aimed at restoring a more natural river system and reducing the risks associated with the aging dam, according to MLive.From a 21-acre impoundment to a flowing riverThe Brooklyn Dam was built in 1939 and held between roughly 4 and 8 feet of water across about 21 acres.Todd Losee, president of Niswander Environmental, said the former impoundment had become stagnant and was dominated by invasive aquatic vegetation.“(It was) pretty stagnant water dominated by invasive aquatic plants, really mucky,” Losee said during a tour of the former dam on Thursday, September 24.Niswander Environmental, which specializes in wetland and stream mitigation projects, worked as a contractor and consultant on the project.The work has changed the course of the water rather than simply eliminating the former dam structure. Most of the old structure remains, but water now flows through an adjacent channel created by sloping the riverbed.The new river path occupies an area where about 18.5 feet of dirt once stood beside the dam.Dam concerns grew after Edenville collapseThe Brooklyn Dam became a greater concern after the Edenville Dam failed in Midland County in 2020.Dan Ross, who purchased the Brooklyn Dam and surrounding property in 2014, began noticing signs that his own structure could potentially fail. He contacted Michigan’s Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy, or EGLE.The agency issued an emergency permit allowing the water behind the dam to be lowered and connected Ross with Niswander Environmental.Lowering the water level was a major undertaking. Losee said it took approximately 43 days to reduce the level by 10 to 12 feet.The River Raisin and Mill Pond water was ultimately redirected away from the high-risk section of the dam.The Kendron Drain also connects to the river.Environmental changes already visibleAccording to the River Raisin Watershed Council, the project is already improving fish movement and restoring native vegetation.It has also removed some invasive aquatic plants that had flourished behind the dam.Additional work remains. Crews plan to construct two more drop structures to lower the river, install a rock-based fish ramp and plant additional shrubs and trees along the waterway.The stone Mill Street bridge over the River Raisin will also be rebuilt as a single-span bridge with stamped, colored concrete.Project officials will continue monitoring water levels as the new river system develops.Resident loses a familiar view but embraces the new riverFor Peggy Hudson, 71, the changes have been personal.Hudson grew up along the River Raisin and bought her childhood home in 2013. She remembers cutting across the ice to get to school during the winter and watching neighbors take their pontoons onto the river in summer.The portion of the river behind her home is now part of the area where the new channel was created.Hudson said she once had several views of the water from her home. Since construction began, the water level has dropped between 5 and 10 feet, making the river much harder to see.“That’s what I’m missing,” Hudson said as she showed a photograph of a sunset reflecting across the river from her backyard before the water level was lowered. “It’s gone.”Despite losing that familiar view, Hudson said she understood why the changes were necessary. Her home sits high enough that she did not require flood insurance, so she was not particularly concerned about flooding.She now plans to build a staircase down toward the river and open her windows so she can hear the faster-moving water.Sediment briefly turned water blackThe project also came with an unexpected visual change.Losee said the release of sediment along the river’s edge was one of the most controversial parts of the work. As the water level dropped, the sediment temporarily turned the river black and created a strong smell.The former dam was connected to 221 Mill Street, a property with a long industrial history. The location was once the site of the Brooklyn village sawmill before later becoming a Ford Motor Co. plant.Could Brooklyn become a model for other dams?The Brooklyn project is being viewed as part of a broader discussion about aging dams across Michigan.Other dams along waterways beyond Brooklyn, including one in Saline, could eventually face similar questions about their future. A dam removal project is also underway in Ypsilanti.Niswander Environmental engineering consultant Ralph Reznick said maintaining aging dams can become increasingly expensive, sometimes making removal a more practical option.But he acknowledged that such decisions can be difficult because dams are often tied to generations of personal memories.“I know your grandfather brought you here fishing, and you proposed to your wife here, and you cried here when your parents died. I know all those things,” Reznick said he wished he could tell residents during public meetings.“But the question is, how much will each one of you be willing to pay to keep the dam? $10 grand a year? $15 grand?”$2 million project could set precedentThe Brooklyn Dam removal was funded through several state and federal grants totaling approximately $2 million.Michigan lawmakers recently passed legislation establishing a Dam Safety Emergency Fund for EGLE and placing the Dam Risk Reduction Grant Program, which helped fund the Brooklyn project, into state law.Losee said the Brooklyn project could provide a model for how those grants can be used in other communities facing aging or high-risk dams.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bentley launches first fully electric Torcal in 107-year history at £173,000, undercutting Ferrari Luce with 375-mile range and 10-80% charging in under 20 minutes
articles.summary: British luxury carmaker Bentley Motors has entered the electric vehicle market with the launch of the all-new Torcal, its first fully electric model in
articles.body: British luxury carmaker Bentley Motors has entered the electric vehicle market with the launch of the all-new Torcal, its first fully electric model in the company’s 107-year history. The new electric SUV marks a significant step for Bentley as the luxury automotive industry continues to test the appetite of affluent buyers for high-performance EVs.The Torcal, which was unveiled in London on Wednesday evening, becomes the fourth model in Bentley’s current line-up alongside the Continental GT, Flying Spur and Bentayga. Designed and engineered at Bentley’s headquarters in Crewe, northwest England, the electric SUV has been developed to combine the brand’s traditional craftsmanship with new electric technology, performance and a completely new design language.The Torcal starts at £173,000, or around $229,000, placing it substantially below Ferrari’s first electric vehicle, the Luce, which carries a reported starting price of around €550,000 ($626,000). Ferrari launched the Luce three months before Bentley’s EV, with its design drawing mixed reactions from some observers and analysts.Bentley says wealthy buyers are increasingly accepting EVsSpeaking to CNBC’s Squawk Box Europe, Bentley Motors chairman and CEO Frank-Steffen Walliser said the Torcal sits at the entry level of Bentley’s price range and has received positive reactions across markets.Walliser said Bentley was not looking at Ferrari’s Luce launch for lessons because the development of a luxury vehicle is a long-term process. He pointed out that Bentley works on a roughly four-year development cycle and cannot change direction simply in response to what another manufacturer has launched.According to Walliser, acceptance of electric cars among Bentley’s wealthy clientele is continuing to grow, with customers becoming increasingly knowledgeable about EV technology.The comments come as several luxury manufacturers reassess their electric strategies. Porsche and Lamborghini, for instance, have scaled back aspects of their EV plans amid weaker-than-expected demand in parts of the luxury electric-car market.Bentley’s approach with the Torcal has been to make the vehicle feel like a Bentley first, regardless of its powertrain. The company says particular attention has been paid to design, driving behaviour, sound and the overall sensory experience.Torcal specifications in detailThe Torcal is a five-metre-long electric SUV and is the shortest four-door Bentley yet produced. It has a wheelbase designed to maximise cabin space while its short overhangs, long bonnet and upright front end give it the powerful stance Bentley wanted for its new design direction.The electric SUV offers a driving range of up to 375 miles, or approximately 600 km, depending on specification and conditions. Bentley says the vehicle can charge from 10% to 80% in less than 20 minutes when connected to a 400kW charging system. The company also says around 100 miles of range can be added in seven minutes.Two versions will be available at launch: the Core and the S.The Core version develops 810bhp and 1,194Nm of torque. It can accelerate from 0 to 60mph in 3.3 seconds and has a top speed of 155mph.The more performance-focused S produces 876bhp and up to 1,350Nm of torque with Launch Control. It can accelerate from 0 to 60mph in just 2.8 seconds, while its top speed rises to 162mph.Bentley says the electric powertrain allows the Torcal to combine supercar-like acceleration with what it describes as year-round usability.The vehicle provides 460 litres of boot space, while a further 90-litre front luggage compartment is available under the bonnet. Its turning circle is 11.1 metres, an important consideration for a vehicle measuring around five metres in length.New Bentley design language debuts with the TorcalThe Torcal represents the production interpretation of Bentley’s EXP 15 concept, which was first revealed in 2025. Its design introduces a new visual direction for the marque while retaining elements intended to connect the electric SUV with Bentley’s heritage.Lead designer Robin Page describes the design process through four key areas: proportion, graphical elements, surface language and detail.The long wheelbase, short overhangs, long bonnet and upright front create what Bentley calls a “powerful stance” and “upright elegance”. The company says the proportions are intended to make the Torcal immediately recognisable as a Bentley despite its new electric architecture.The front features an illuminated diamond grille and advanced lighting elements. The rear graphics form what Bentley describes as a prestigious shield, while several design cues reference the EXP 15 concept and historic Bentley models, including the Continental T.Rather than relying on numerous character lines, Bentley has used a more sculptural approach. The surfaces taper towards the rear, creating what the company describes as the appearance of a “resting beast”.The diamond pattern seen on the exterior continues into the cabin, creating a visual link between the outside and inside of the vehicle.Cabin combines leather, wood, wool and aluminium with digital technologyInside, the Torcal blends traditional Bentley materials with modern technology.The dashboard takes inspiration from a wing and combines leather, wood or veneer and aluminium. Bentley has retained physical controls in key areas, including the centre console and steering wheel, while curved OLED displays provide the main digital interface.The seats offer 16-way adjustment, along with heating, ventilation, adjustable bolsters and massage functions. Optional postural adjustment and smart climate functions are also available.A wellness-focused seat function can provide leg massage, adding another element to Bentley’s emphasis on long-distance comfort.The company has also placed considerable emphasis on sustainable material choices. The cabin can use leather, wood, wool and aluminium, including what Bentley describes as the world’s first 100% Merino wool automotive fabric, which is certified by the Responsible Wool Standard.Sustainably sourced walnut offcuts are also used in the interior.For additional practicality, Bentley has introduced power-folding rear seats for the first time in the model.Four Experience modes change the character of the carThe Torcal features four Experience modes that alter various aspects of the vehicle, including lighting, sound, climate, airflow and the amount of digital information presented to the driver.Comfort mode is designed around a calmer environment and a more relaxed experience, including what Bentley describes as a digital detox approach.Sport mode, meanwhile, increases the intensity of the experience with a more immersive soundtrack and changes to the lighting and other cabin elements.Facial-recognition technology can also identify individual occupants and automatically adjust settings such as the seat, steering wheel and certain advanced driver-assistance system preferences.The Torcal uses a network of 25 radars, sensors and cameras to support its driver-assistance and vehicle-monitoring systems.Bentley recreates engine character for its electric SUVOne of the more distinctive aspects of the Torcal is its approach to sound.Instead of leaving the cabin silent, Bentley has created the Bentley Dynamic Symphony, an artificial soundtrack designed around the rhythms and character associated with the company’s historic combustion engines.The sound incorporates elements inspired by Bentley’s 6¾-litre V8, combined with drums, viola and bass guitar.The soundtrack is calibrated to the vehicle’s torque demand and speed, with the intensity, volume and feedback increasing when the driver selects Sport mode.Bentley has also developed a more advanced audio system for the cabin. The standard system produces 620 watts through 16 speakers, while the optional system delivers 1,780 watts through 28 speakers with Dolby Atmos. The upgraded system also incorporates kinaesthetic seat shakers and speakers positioned in the front headrests.S version brings a more aggressive exteriorThe Torcal S receives additional styling changes to distinguish it from the Core version.These include black exterior brightware, black mirror caps, darker rear lamps, rear diffusers and sportier side sills. The front bumper also receives additional strakes, while red brake calipers add another performance-oriented visual element.Inside, the S introduces its own colour split, quilting and stitching treatments.While the S offers the highest output at 876bhp, Bentley says the focus is not simply on outright acceleration. The company has attempted to combine the additional performance with the comfort, refinement and usability traditionally associated with its luxury grand tourers and SUVs.Bentley wants the Torcal to remain a Bentley firstThe Torcal arrives at a critical point for the luxury EV market, where manufacturers are balancing increasingly powerful electric drivetrains with changing customer expectations.Bentley’s first fully electric model was originally expected to arrive earlier, but its launch was pushed back amid softer demand for luxury electric vehicles.The company is now betting that its established design language, handcrafted interior, high performance and focus on sound and sensory experience can make the transition to electric power feel familiar to existing Bentley customers.With a starting price of £173,000, a range of up to 375 miles, charging from 10% to 80% in less than 20 minutes and as much as 876bhp in S specification, the Torcal represents Bentley’s attempt to bring electric propulsion into its traditional luxury performance formula.The model is expected to go on sale by the end of the year, although the extensive range of available options can push the final price significantly higher.You use AI every day. articles.title: Massachusetts Communist Party chapter attacks Boston Globe over lesbian bar story
articles.summary: A Communist Party chapter accused The Boston Globe of courting far-right outrage with its reporting on a Greenfield, Massachusetts, lesbian bar's mask policy change.
articles.body: A Massachusetts chapter of the Communist Party took aim at The Boston Globe on Thursday over its reporting on a lesbian bar that has been criticized for lifting its mask mandate for just one night a week. The Boston Globe published an article about Last Ditch, a lesbian bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts, that sparked community backlash after it announced it would be making Saturdays mask-optional. The community responded with accusations of ableism and some even called for a boycott of the business. The Western Massachusetts CPUSA posted a statement on X and on its website calling for solidarity with "the queer and transgender people of our region facing heightened national scrutiny." On X, the graphic that included the statement suggested the Globe was part of "MAGA Media," saying, "The Boston Globe, an ally of corporate lobbies across the state, stands on the other side. After endorsing notoriously transphobic Rep. Seth Moulton’s failed Senate campaign, the Globe has pivoted to courting the outrage of the national extreme right and directing it at our region." BOSTON GLOBE OP-ED SAYS VIOLENCE AGAINST TRANSGENDER PEOPLE IS 'GOING DOWN' DESPITE ACTIVIST CLAIMS The statement argued the article about the Greenfield lesbian bar was "not newsworthy." "The September 22nd article is not newsworthy, except in the context of the upcoming midterm elections in which transgender rights are a central political issue, as well as a far-right national consumer base which makes the scrutiny of transgender lives profitable," it read. "The Western Massachusetts CPUSA rejects the use of conflicts among LGBTQIA+ people and organizations as a tool of division by the extreme right. We reaffirm our solidarity with all those struggling against the genocide of transgender people," the statement added. The Boston Globe's director of communications, Adam Bagni responded to the criticism in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The Boston Globe is locally owned, and our newsroom makes editorial decisions independently, guided by our commitment to fair and accurate reporting," the statement said. DOUG SCHOEN: WHY DEMOCRATS CANNOT BREAK FREE FROM THE FAR LEFT’S TRANSGENDER DEMANDS Some critics accused Last Ditch's owners of putting disabled people at risk and compared the policy change to a "mass disabling event" and a "eugenicist" attack while also wishing violence against the establishment, according to the Globe. "I hope your venue gets firebombed for robbing my fellow immunocompromised people of their Saturday plans just to scrape extra revenue from ablists [sic]," one commenter wrote on the bar's social media post announcing the change. "People like you kill disabled people in the name of your own leisure and convenience," wrote another. "Just say you’re being complicit in a mass disabling event and get it over with," a third said. "When y'all close, let the record state it was ableism + complying in advance, because that's what it is," another wrote. HOW THE MEDIA, IN THE DIGITAL AGE, HELP FUEL A CLIMATE OF ANGER AND VIOLENCE This comes years after the COVID-19 pandemic was declared over by the federal government in 2023. State and local governments, as well as most businesses across the country, lifted masking requirements several years ago. Additionally, Greenfield had not reported a COVID-19 case in more than two months, according to the Globe. The backlash came as the bar was already struggling financially under its unusual business model, which includes rules such as "Nobody will be barred from entry due to lack of funds." "It is with love we inform our immunocompromised disabled divas we will be opening Saturday nights as mask optional," Last Ditch wrote in an August Instagram post that ignited the backlash. The bar first attempted to ease tensions and apologize for its post, writing: "We are sorry for our passive and dismissive tone of our change to the norms and schedule impacting the most intersectional of us. We understand everyone faces different intersections, and we are always working to consider all needs fully." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE On Thursday, the bar called the Globe's article "abysmal journalism" in a post on Instagram. Last Ditch also issued a call for donations and support, saying, "Operating a venue is expensive, especially when prioritizing community over profit. Our owners work on a volunteer basis (that's right, none of our owners receive a wage or salary) so every dollar we receive can be reinvested in Last Ditch to pay employees & performers, restock product, make necessary renovations to the space, advertise, and so. much. more." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' Landon Mion contributed to this report.

articles.title: E-bikes seized by police sold on at auction, BBC finds
articles.summary: Thousands are confiscated annually because they are suspected of being driven illegally or used in a crime - most are destroyed, but last year police sold at least 161.
articles.body:
E-bikes seized by police forces in the UK are being sold on at auction, despite some fears they could end up back in the hands of criminals, the BBC can reveal.

Thousands are confiscated annually because they are suspected of being driven illegally, or used in a crime.

Most of them are later destroyed, but a BBC investigation has found some are sold on to members of the public in online auctions.

Across the UK, police sold 161 e-bikes last year and 54 in 2024, although the real number could be higher because not every force responded to the BBC's Freedom of Information request.

The figure includes electrically-assisted pedal cycles, which look similar to bicycles and have a motor that kicks in as a rider pedals, as well as electric motorbikes, which are usually more powerful and are propelled only by their motor.

Six forces responded to say e-bikes they had seized had been sold, including large forces such as West Midlands Police and Police Scotland.

When approached by the BBC, some of the forces said they had now ended the practice, but others defended it as a way of putting "money back into policing".

E-bikes have become controversial because some think they are linked to crime and anti-social behaviour.

Recent BBC reporting has highlighted cases across the country of balaclava-clad young men riding illegally on footpaths and intimidating residents.

Police Scotland, which covers the whole country, says it sends seized e-bikes to an accredited recycler who may then decide to auction them, with money going back to the force. Last year 93 e-bikes seized by Police Scotland were sold, more than any other force.

Two e-bikes seized by West Yorkshire Police last year were sold at auction. The force said any money raised from the auctions was split between the force and the West Yorkshire Combined Authority, and said some cash went to "local good causes". All of those sold were "legally compliant", they added.

West Midlands Police, which sold 12 e-bikes last year, said the "vast majority" of seized bikes were destroyed, with a "small number" sold "via an independent auction company so that the money can be put back into policing".

The BBC found some forces had also sold e-scooters. It is illegal to use a privately-owned e-scooter on public property, although owning an e-scooter is not illegal.

Durham Constabulary sold three of them last year, and West Mercia Police sold one. West Mercia's force also sold 24 e-bikes.

Both forces told the BBC they have recently reviewed their policy and they will no longer sell e-bikes or e-scooters.

Clive Grunshaw, the Police and Crime Commissioner for Lancashire said: "There's nowhere apart from [a] back garden that these scooters can be legally used, so it's a confused message," he said.

He urged police forces to stop selling e-bikes, which he said have become the "transport of choice for drug gangs" because they are "so difficult to catch".

He suspects that some criminals whose vehicles are seized simply try to buy them back from auction websites.

Grunshaw worries some criminals are buying legally compliant e-bikes from police and then giving them illegal modifications.

Legal electric pedal bikes are restricted so they cannot drive faster than 15.5mph, but criminals can buy "tuning kits" online, often from eastern Europe, allowing some to travel faster than 40mph.

Durham Constabulary, which sold 29 e-bikes last year, told the BBC they had recently reviewed its policy, and they "will now be crushed without exception".

Greater Manchester Police sold one e-bike last year.

Police tend to sell the vehicles through commercial auction websites like Raw2k, a company listed by several forces.

The website regularly advertises e-bikes as "sold at the direction of police", including a Chinese-manufactured electric dirt bike that it says was auctioned from Falkirk earlier this month, with an opening price of £250 (much less than the £3,295 listed as the retail price for a new model).

articles.title: As Merz scrambles for support, Germany's identity crisis is laid bare
articles.summary: Voters are turning away from the centre in Germany as fears grow about the economy and migration.
articles.body:
A set of bumper local elections has thrown Germany, and its government, off balance.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz may now be a man on borrowed time. His coalition government is in crisis.

But this breakdown of business as usual in Germany has been brewing for years.

It's a nation wrestling with new, uncomfortable and unresolved realities.

Think of certain stereotypes about Germany, and think again.

A country dominated by boring, consensus-driven politics? Not any more.

A confident, powerhouse economy at the cutting edge of car-making? Yesterday's story.

A nation that can be used as a byword for impressive efficiency? The trains don't even run on time.

Many Germans I've spoken to feel their nation has drifted away from the things that once anchored their identity.

And the question of what next is, as yet, unanswered.

That uncertainty is currently embodied by a beleaguered chancellor weakened by bruising regional election results.

In the last fortnight, Friedrich Merz's party was beaten to first place in Berlin, pummelled in the polls in Saxony-Anhalt and pushed out of parliament altogether in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

A lifeline for Merz is that no-one, within his own centre-right CDU party, is yet willing to challenge the chancellor openly despite persistent rumours of a Kanzlertausch (chancellor swap).

But he is on thin ice, with record low approval ratings among voters who often describe him as arrogant and out of touch.

It is a problem that in government circles is sometimes more politely referred to as a "communication" issue.

Those who back the Chancellor say it is time to double down on much-needed reforms, alongside its centre-left SPD coalition partner, and find a better way of talking to people.

Swapping chancellors is not the answer as anyone would face the "same challenges", argues Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy spokesperson in parliament for Merz's CDU and its sister party, the CSU.

Hardt pointed out that the CDU/CSU fared far better in other regional elections earlier this year, when we spoke minutes after Merz addressed party lawmakers at a closed-door meeting in the Bundestag.

"I think Friedrich Merz knows about his deficits," says Hardt. "He will work on him and we will work on us as (a) party. And hopefully we will convince the people in the next months that we are on the right way."

Merz came to power in 2025, promising to get tough on immigration and boost Germany's ailing economy.

He appeared to offer a dynamism that might act as an antidote to the former dull, unhappy drumbeat of centre-left leader Olaf Scholz's bickering three-way coalition.

And Merz's allies would claim he has had some success.

This week, leading economic institutes raised the country's growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 above 1% while illegal entries into Germany – and Europe – are down year on year.

But that will not eliminate public anxieties, on either issue.

Households and businesses continue to endure high energy costs while fears persist that China is cannibalising German industry, including its iconic car sector.

It is a brutal reversal of Germany's old recipe for success: cheap Russian gas that powered a booming export-driven economy.

And when it comes to immigration, the focus is now less on new arrivals and more on concerns about public safety, welfare costs and integration.

While there are local exceptions, voters appear to be losing faith in Germany's two principal governing parties (CDU and SPD).

Enter the rising force in German politics, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD): a party that alarms security officials with its Russia-friendly stance and contains regional branches that are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence.

Smears and misrepresentations, argues the AfD, as it claimed its third victory ever in a state election last Sunday in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-West Pomerania.

Its co-leader, Alice Weidel, told me this week that Friedrich Merz's days were numbered.

The AfD has survived numerous scandals in recent years to now top the polls nationwide, at around 28%. It carries the swagger of a party making the political weather.

It has capitalised on a nostalgia for the past alongside an anxiety in the present as it consolidates its strongholds in the former communist east.

An AfD placard I saw in Berlin read "Berlin braucht Ordnung" (Berlin needs order). It is the as yet untested promise that this party can bring back a lost sense of stability.

But in Germany's capital it was in fact Die Linke (the Left) that topped the polls last Sunday in a further blow to the country's traditional "big tent" parties.

The victory has put fresh scrutiny on Die Linke, as it faces allegations of antisemitism. The party leadership has insisted it is committed to protecting Jewish life.

This round of regional elections has encapsulated the country's fault lines: the eroding support for Germany's political centre, and a polarising debate on the AfD.

Rarely in post-war Germany has a set of local polls generated so much upheaval at home and interest abroad.
